title: Strings: the methods behind the traps
description: The String and StringBuilder methods interviews probe — strip versus trim on Unicode whitespace, lines and isBlank, in-place builder edits, surrogate pairs and code points, String.join, index arithmetic with indexOf/lastIndexOf, the chars() IntStream, and replace (literal) versus replaceAll (regex). Complements javabootcamp's string drills (vowel loops, == vs equals, StringBuilder building, split/format/regex parsing) with the method contracts behind the classic traps.

exercises.title: The space that trim could not see
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Usernames pasted from a Japanese form still have 'spaces' around them after `trim()`. Why, and what should we call instead?"

**Why it works.** `trim()` predates Unicode-aware text handling: it removes only characters whose code is `<= U+0020` (ASCII space and control characters). `strip()` (Java 11) removes every leading and trailing character for which `Character.isWhitespace` is true — that includes the ideographic space `U+3000`, which is whitespace but far above `U+0020`. A third case to know (and that the tests check): the non-breaking space `U+00A0` is removed by NEITHER — it is above `U+0020`, and `Character.isWhitespace` deliberately returns false for it.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `clean(String raw)` → `raw` with Unicode whitespace stripped from both ends, then lower-cased with `Locale.ROOT`.
- `legacyTrim(String raw)` → `raw` trimmed the old way (`trim()`), kept for comparison.

**Worked example.** `clean("　x　")` returns `"x"`, while `legacyTrim("　x　")` returns `"　x　"` unchanged.
exercises.explanation:
`trim` knows ASCII; `strip` knows Unicode whitespace.

For `"　x　"`:
- `trim()` removes only characters `<= U+0020`; `U+3000` is far above that → the string comes back unchanged
- `strip()` asks `Character.isWhitespace('　')` → true → both ends are removed → `"x"`, and lower-casing leaves `"x"`
- for `" x"` neither method removes the non-breaking space: it is above `U+0020` and `isWhitespace` is false for it

Kinship: javabootcamp's string drills never touch whitespace classification; this contract is unowned there. In an interview, "use `strip`, and normalise `U+00A0` explicitly if your input can contain it" is the complete answer.
hints: Look up the code point of the ideographic space and compare it with what trim was designed for.
String.strip uses Character.isWhitespace; String.trim only removes characters at or below U+0020.
trim only knows the old ASCII range while strip asks the Unicode whitespace test — and the non-breaking space fools them both

exercises.title: Lines, every flavour of them
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A config blob arrives with Windows and Unix line endings mixed, plus blank and whitespace-only lines. Give me the meaningful lines without writing a regex."

**Why it works.** `String.lines()` (Java 11) splits on every line terminator — `\n`, `\r` and `\r\n` — and never yields the terminators themselves; a trailing terminator does not create an extra empty line, and the empty string has ZERO lines. `isBlank()` is true for an empty string or one made only of whitespace. Chaining `lines()` → `filter(!isBlank)` → `strip` replaces the split-by-regex-then-trim dance.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `nonBlankLines(String text)` → the lines that are not blank, each stripped, in order.
- `lineCount(String text)` → how many lines `text` has, blank ones included.

**Worked example.** `nonBlankLines("a\n \n\nb\r\nc")` returns `["a", "b", "c"]`, and `lineCount` of the same text is **5**.
exercises.explanation:
`lines()` understands every terminator; `isBlank()` understands whitespace.

For `"a\n \n\nb\r\nc"`:
- `lines()` yields `"a"`, `" "`, `""`, `"b"`, `"c"` — the `\r\n` is one terminator → `lineCount` is **5**
- `isBlank` drops `" "` and `""` → `"a"`, `"b"`, `"c"`, already stripped → `["a", "b", "c"]`
- a hand-rolled `split("\n")` would have left `"b\r"` with a stray carriage return

Kinship: javabootcamp 18 (parsing and framing) splits with explicit limits and delimiters; the built-in `lines`/`isBlank` pair is unowned there. In an interview, knowing that `"".lines()` is empty and that `\r\n` counts once saves an off-by-one.
hints: Splitting on "\n" by hand leaves carriage returns behind on Windows input.
String.lines splits on \n, \r and \r\n; String.isBlank is true for empty or whitespace-only strings; String.strip trims each survivor.
lines already understands every newline flavour and isBlank already understands Unicode blanks — chain them instead of splitting by hand

exercises.title: Editing a card number in place
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Mask all but the last four digits of a card number, and reverse a string — without building either from scratch character by character."

**Why it works.** A `StringBuilder` is a mutable buffer you can EDIT, not just append to. `replace(start, end, str)` swaps the index window `[start, end)` for `str` (an empty window just inserts, so `replace(2, 2, "")` changes nothing); `reverse()` flips the whole buffer in place (and keeps surrogate pairs intact). `"*".repeat(n)` makes the mask.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `redact(String s, int from, int to)` → `s` with the characters in `[from, to)` replaced by the same number of `*`.
- `reversed(String s)` → `s` reversed.

**Worked example.** `redact("4111222233334444", 0, 12)` returns `"************4444"`.
exercises.explanation:
`StringBuilder` edits; it does not only append.

For `redact("4111222233334444", 0, 12)`:
- the window `[0, 12)` is 12 characters, so the mask is `"*".repeat(12)`
- `replace(0, 12, "************")` swaps those 12 characters for 12 stars
- the last four characters `"4444"` are untouched → `"************4444"`

Kinship: javabootcamp 04/01 builds a receipt with `append` and `repeat`; this drill is in-place EDITING (`replace`, `reverse`) on an existing buffer. In an interview, `new StringBuilder(s).reverse()` is the one-liner expected for "reverse a string".
hints: Copy the string into a mutable buffer first — a String itself can never change.
StringBuilder.replace takes a start, an exclusive end and the replacement; StringBuilder.reverse needs no arguments.
a builder edits in place — replace swaps an index window and reverse flips the whole buffer

exercises.title: The emoji that counted as two
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our 'first character' preview turns a leading emoji into a `?` box, and the character counter says `a🙂b` is 4 long. Explain both bugs."

**Why it works.** A Java `String` is a sequence of UTF-16 code UNITS (`char`s). Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane — like 🙂 (`U+1F642`) — take TWO units, a surrogate pair (`🙂`). So `length()` counts units (`"a🙂b"` → 4), and `substring(0, 1)` cuts the pair in half, leaving a lone high surrogate. `codePointCount(0, length())` counts real characters (code points), and `offsetByCodePoints(0, 1)` tells you the char index just after the first code point — the safe place to cut.

**Your task.** Implement three methods:
- `charLength(String s)` → the number of UTF-16 code units.
- `glyphCount(String s)` → the number of code points.
- `firstGlyph(String s)` → the first code point as a String (both units of a surrogate pair). `s` is non-empty.

**Worked example.** For `"a🙂b"` (written `"a🙂b"` in the tests), `charLength` is **4** and `glyphCount` is **3**.
exercises.explanation:
`length()` counts code units; code-point methods count characters.

For `"a🙂b"` (`a🙂b`):
- the units are `a`, `\uD83D`, `\uDE42`, `b` → `charLength` **4**
- the high/low surrogates form one code point `U+1F642` → `glyphCount` **3**
- for `firstGlyph("🙂b")`, `offsetByCodePoints(0, 1)` is 2, so `substring(0, 2)` keeps the whole pair; `substring(0, 1)` would have kept a lone `\uD83D`

Kinship: javabootcamp never touches surrogate pairs (01/08 does char arithmetic on ASCII only). In an interview, "`length()` is UTF-16 units, not characters" is the sentence that separates a careful answer from a buggy truncation.
hints: Some characters need two chars — try printing the length of a string holding a single emoji.
String.codePointCount counts code points over a char range; String.offsetByCodePoints converts a code-point step into a char index.
length counts UTF-16 units while codePointCount counts real characters — step by code points when slicing near an emoji

exercises.title: Joining without the trailing slash
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Build a URL path from segments and a query string from ordered parameters. No trailing `/` or `&`, please."

**Why it works.** `String.join(delimiter, elements)` puts the delimiter BETWEEN elements only — never before the first or after the last — so there is no "remove the last separator" bookkeeping. A single element comes back unchanged and an empty collection gives `""`. Iterating a `LinkedHashMap` visits entries in insertion order, so the query keeps the caller's parameter order.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `pathOf(List<String> parts)` → the parts joined with `/`.
- `query(LinkedHashMap<String, String> params)` → `key=value` pairs, in the map's order, joined with `&`.

**Worked example.** `pathOf(List.of("api", "v2", "users"))` returns `"api/v2/users"`.
exercises.explanation:
`String.join` only puts separators between elements.

For `pathOf(["api", "v2", "users"])`:
- the delimiter goes between `api`/`v2` and `v2`/`users` — two slashes for three parts
- nothing is added before `api` or after `users` → `"api/v2/users"`
- a hand-written loop that appends `part + "/"` would end with `"users/"` and need trimming

Kinship: drill 01 of the collectors module does the same with `Collectors.joining` inside a stream; this is the static `String.join` over a ready-made collection. In an interview, reaching for `String.join` instead of a loop with a "first element" flag is the expected idiom.
hints: A loop that appends a separator after every element always leaves one too many.
String.join takes the delimiter first, then an Iterable of strings; a LinkedHashMap iterates its entries in insertion order.
String join takes the delimiter first and spares you the trailing-separator bookkeeping

exercises.title: Slicing by anchors
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Without `split` or a regex: get the domain of an email, the extension of a file name, and the text between two markers."

**Why it works.** `indexOf(x)` finds the FIRST occurrence of an anchor, `lastIndexOf(x)` the LAST; both answer `-1` when the anchor is absent — and that `-1` must be checked before slicing, or `substring` throws or silently returns the wrong window. `indexOf(x, from)` resumes the search after a position, which is how you find a closing marker after its opener. The extension of `archive.tar.gz` is `gz`: it hangs off the LAST dot.

**Your task.** Implement three methods:
- `domainOf(String email)` → everything after the `@` (inputs contain exactly one `@`).
- `extensionOf(String file)` → everything after the last `.`; `""` when there is no dot or the name ends with a dot.
- `between(String s, String open, String close)` → the text between the first `open` and the first `close` after it; `""` when either is missing.

**Worked example.** `extensionOf("archive.tar.gz")` returns `"gz"`.
exercises.explanation:
Find the anchor, check for `-1`, then slice.

For `extensionOf("archive.tar.gz")`:
- `lastIndexOf('.')` is 11 (the dot before `gz`); `indexOf('.')` would have found 7 and returned `"tar.gz"`
- 11 is neither `-1` nor the last index → `substring(12)` → `"gz"`
- for `"README"` the index is `-1` → `""` instead of the whole name

Kinship: javabootcamp 04/02 parses with `split`; index arithmetic without split or regex is the distinct, allocation-free idiom. In an interview, saying "check for `-1` before you slice" out loud is half the credit.
hints: Decide which occurrence of the anchor you need — the first one or the last one.
String.indexOf and String.lastIndexOf return -1 when absent; indexOf has an overload taking a start position; substring takes a start and an exclusive end.
find the anchor with indexOf or its last-occurrence twin and slice with substring — minus one means the anchor was never there

exercises.title: A string as a stream of ints
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Sum the digits embedded in an order code, and count how often a character occurs — as a stream, no index loop."

**Why it works.** `String.chars()` returns an `IntStream` of the string's `char` values (as ints). `filter(Character::isDigit)` keeps the digits, and `c - '0'` turns the character code of a digit into its value (`'7' - '0'` is 7). `sum()` and `count()` finish the job. (These inputs are ASCII; for other scripts you would use `Character.digit`.)

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `digitSum(String s)` → the sum of the decimal digits in `s` (0 when there are none).
- `countOf(String s, char target)` → how many times `target` occurs in `s`.

**Worked example.** `digitSum("a1b22")` returns **5**.
exercises.explanation:
`chars()` turns the string into an `IntStream`.

For `digitSum("a1b22")`:
- `chars()` yields the codes of `a`, `1`, `b`, `2`, `2`
- `filter(Character::isDigit)` keeps `'1'`, `'2'`, `'2'`
- `map(c -> c - '0')` gives 1, 2, 2 → `sum()` **5**

Kinship: javabootcamp 01/01 counts vowels with a LOOP; this drill is the `chars()` IntStream idiom itself. In an interview, remember that `chars()` yields ints — `mapToObj(c -> (char) c)` is needed if you want characters back.
hints: A string can hand you its characters as a stream of int codes.
String.chars gives an IntStream; Character.isDigit works as an IntPredicate; IntStream has sum and count.
chars streams the string as ints — filter on the character tests and subtract the zero digit to get values

exercises.title: The dot that matched everything
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We wanted to turn `a.b.c` into `a*b*c` and got `*****`. What happened?"

**Why it works.** The two methods look alike but read their first argument differently. `replace(CharSequence, CharSequence)` is LITERAL: it replaces every occurrence of exactly that text. `replaceAll(String regex, String)` COMPILES its first argument as a regular expression — and in a regex, a bare `.` means "any character". So `"a.b.c".replaceAll(".", "*")` replaces all five characters and returns `"*****"`. Use `replace` for plain text; use `replaceAll` when you genuinely want a pattern, such as `\\s+` for "one or more whitespace characters".

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `starDots(String s)` → every literal `.` replaced by `*`.
- `collapseSpaces(String s)` → every run of whitespace (spaces, tabs, …) replaced by a single space.

**Worked example.** `starDots("a.b.c")` returns `"a*b*c"`.
exercises.explanation:
`replace` is literal; `replaceAll` is a regex.

For `starDots("a.b.c")` with `replace(".", "*")`:
- the two literal dots are the only matches → `"a*b*c"`
- with `replaceAll(".", "*")` the pattern `.` matches `a`, `.`, `b`, `.`, `c` → `"*****"`
- `collapseSpaces("a   b\t c")`: `\\s+` matches `"   "` and `"\t "` → each becomes one space → `"a b c"`

Kinship: javabootcamp 04/04 drills regex anchors with Pattern/Matcher; this is the replace-is-literal / replaceAll-is-regex split that bites people who never meant to write a regex. In an interview, also name `Pattern.quote` as the fix when a literal must go through a regex API.
hints: Only one of the two methods treats its first argument as a pattern.
String.replace takes CharSequences and is literal; String.replaceAll takes a regex where . means any character and \s+ means a whitespace run.
replace treats its argument as plain text while replaceAll compiles it — a bare dot in the second one matches everything
